<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A Hilbert $A$-module X is a $C^*$-correspondence if it is equipped with a $*$-homomorphism $\varphi_X : A \xrightarrow[]{} \mathcal{L}(X)$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A representation $(\psi^1, \psi^0)$ of a $C^*$-correspondence on a $C^*$-algebra $B$ is a pair of maps $\psi^0 : A \xrightarrow[]{} B$ is a $*$-homomorphisms and $\psi^1: X \xrightarrow[]{} B$ is a linear map such that the following natural conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\psi^1(x)^* \psi^1(y) = \psi^0(\langle x , y\rangle_A)$
    \item $\psi^0(a)\psi^1(x) = \psi^1(\varphi_X(a) x)$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $C^*$-correspondence over $A$. Then the Katsura ideal $J_X$ is:

\begin{align*}
    J_X &= \varphi_X^{-1} (\mathcal{K(X)}) \cap (ker\varphi_X)^{\perp}  \\
        &= \{ a \in A \ | \ \varphi_X(a) \in \mathcal{K}(X) \text{ and } ab = 0 \text{ for all } b \in ker\varphi_X \}
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition~3.4]{katsura_c-algebras_2004})
A representation $(\psi^1,\psi^0)$ of a C*-correspondence $X$ over $A$ on a C*-algebra $B$ is {\em covariant} if $\psi^0(a)=\psi^{(1)}(\varphi_X(a))$ for all $a\in J_X$, where $\psi^{(1)}(\theta_{\eta,\xi}) = t^1(\xi)^*t^1(\eta)$
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition~3.5]{katsura_c-algebras_2004}, cf.~\cite{voiculescu_free_1996})
The {\em Cuntz--Pimsner algebra} $\mathcal{O}_X$ associated to a correspondence $X$ over $A$ is the C*-algebra $C^*(t^1_X,t^0_X)$ generated by the universal covariant representation $(t^1_X,t^0_X)$ of $(X,A)$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
If $E^0, E^1$ are discrete, we recover the usual graph $C^*$-algebras.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
If $X$ is a locally compact space and $\sigma : X \xrightarrow[]{} X$ is a homeomorphism on $X$, then the topological graph algebra corresponding to the topological graph $(X,X, s= id_X, r = \sigma)$ is the homeomorphism $C^*$-algebra $C_0(X) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition~2.3]{katsura_class_2006-1})
An \textit{admissible pair} $\rho = (Y^0,Z^0)$ is a pair of closed subsets of $E^0$ such that $Y^0$ is invariant and $Z^0$ is such that $Y^0_{\rm sg}\subseteq Z^0\subseteq E^0_{\rm sg}\cap Y^0$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{idealclass}
{\rm (\cite[Theorem~3.19]{katsura_class_2006-1})}
For a topological graph $E$, the assignment $I\mapsto \rho_I=(Y^0_I,Z^0_I)$ and $\rho=(Y^0,Z^0)\mapsto I_\rho$ give rise to an inclusion-reversing one-to-one correspondence between the set of gauge-invariant ideals of $C^*(E)$ and the set of admissible pairs in $E^0$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition~5.1]{katsura_class_2006-1})
Let $V \subseteq E^0$. Then $V$ is called \textit{hereditary} if $r(s^{-1}(V)) \subseteq V$ and \textit{saturated} if for $v \in E^0_{rg}$ with $r(s^{-1}(v) \subseteq V$ implies $v \in V$. For $V \subseteq E^0$, define:
\begin{align*}
    H(V) = \bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n((s^{n})^{-1}(V))
\end{align*}
and,
$S(V) = \bigcup V_k$ with $V_0 = V$ and $V_{k+1}$ defined inductively as:
\begin{align*}
    V_{k+1} = V_k \cup \{ v \in E^0_{rg} \vert r(s^{-1}(v)) \subseteq V \}
\end{align*}
\label{hss}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{factorkatsura}
(\cite[Definition~2.1, Definition~2.6]{katsura_class_2006})
Let $E$ and $F$ be topological graphs. Then, a \textit{regular factor map} $m : E \xrightarrow[]{} F$ is a pair of proper continuous maps, $m^1:E^1\xrightarrow[]{} F^1$ and $m^0:E^0 \xrightarrow[]{} F^0$ such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(F1)] $r_F(m^1(e))=m^0(r_E(e))$ and $s_F(m^1(e))=m^0(s_E(e))$ for all $e\in E^1$.
\item[(F2)] If $x\in F^1$ and $v\in E^0$ satisfies $r_F(x)=m^0(v)$, then there exists a unique element $e\in E^1$ such that $m^1(e)=x$ and $r_E(e)=v$.
\item[(F3)] $m^0(E^0_{\rm sg})\subseteq F^0_{\rm sg}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The definition of regularity in~\cite[Definition~2.6]{katsura_class_2006} is slightly different. However, it is equivalent to our definition due to~\cite[Lemma~2.7]{katsura_class_2006}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{functc*}
{\rm (\cite[Proposition~2.9]{katsura_class_2006})}
Let $m:E\to F$ be a regular factor map. Then there exists a unique gauge-equivariant $*$-homomorphism $\mu:C^*(F)\to C^*(E)$ such that $\mu\circ t_F^i=\mu^i$, $i=0,1$, where $\mu^0$ and $\mu^1$ are defined by~\eqref{precomp}.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
A path in $e = (e^1,e^2, \dots, e^n)$ in $E^n$ with $n \geq 1$ is a \textit{loop} if $r(e^n) = s(e^1)$. A vertex in $e$ is called a base point. A loop is said to be \textit{without exits} if $s^{-1}(s(e^k)) = e^k$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
A topological graph $E$ is called \textit{topologically free} if the set of base points of loops without exits has empty interior.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Similar results for general Cuntz-Pimsner algebras appear in \cite{paulovicks_cuntz-krieger_2025}, referred to as Condition (S).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
(\cite[Theorem 5.12]{katsura_class_2004}
If $E$ is topological graph such that it is topologically free and $B$ is any $C^*$-algebra. Then if $\rho : C^*(E) \xrightarrow[]{} B$ is a $*$-homomorphism such that $\rho \vert_{t^0(C_0(E^0))}$ is injective, then $\rho$ is injective.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition 2.1]{dandrea_quantum_2026})
An \textit{unpointed Waldhausen category} is a category $\mathcal{C}$ with an initial object $\empty$ and a terminal object $\star$, with two distinguished classes of morphisms: $Cof$ of \textit{cofibrations} denoted by $\xhookrightarrow{}$ and $Weq$ of \textit{weak equivalences} denoted by $\xrightarrow[]{\sim}$ such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(Iso)] Isomorphisms are both cofibrations and weak equivalences
\item[(Com)] $Cof$ and $Weq$ are closed under composition
\item[(Cof)] For any object, the unique morphism $\empty \xhookrightarrow{} X$ is a cofibration.  Furthermore, if $X \xhookrightarrow{} Y$ is a cofibration and $X \xrightarrow[]{} \tilde{X}$ is any morphism then the pushout $\tilde{X} \xhookrightarrow{} \tilde{X} \bigcup_X Y$ is also a cofibration.
\item[(Weq)] Given any commutative diagram of the form:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	Z \& X \& Y \\
	{\tilde{Z}} \& {\tilde{X}} \& {\tilde{Y}}
	\arrow["{\sim}", from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-1]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\sim}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\sim}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
the induced maps on the pushouts $Z \bigsqcup_X Y \xrightarrow[]{} \tilde{Z} \bigsqcup_{\tilde{X}} \tilde{Y}$ is a weak equivalence.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition 2.2]{dandrea_quantum_2026})
An unpointed Waldhausen category is a \textit{cw-Waldhausen category} such that the following are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(cw-W)] 
For every pushout diagram,
    \[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\& {\tilde{\tilde{Z}}} \& \\
	{\tilde{Y}} \&\& {\tilde{Z}} \\
	\& Y
	\arrow["{\tilde{j}}", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\tilde{h}}"', from=2-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow["g", from=3-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow["j"', hook, from=3-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
 with $j$ being a cofibration, then $\tilde{h}$ is a weak equivalence iff g is one as well.
 \item[(2/3)] For every commutative diagram of the form
 \[
 \begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	X \& Y \& Z
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[curve={height=12pt}, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
with any two of the morphisms being weak equivalences implies the third one sn a weak equivalence as well.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition 2.3]{dandrea_quantum_2026})
An object $X$ in a cw-Waldhausen category is weakly contractible if the unique morphism $X \xrightarrow[]{} \star$ is a weak equivalence.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
A \textit{cw-Waldhausen symmetric monoidal category} $\mathcal{C}$ is a category which is both a cw-Waldhausen category and a symmetric monoidal category with the terminal object as a monoidal unit together with a fully distinguished subcategory $\mathcal{C}^{\times}$ such that the following are true:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(Con-Weq)] Any morphism $X \xrightarrow[]{} Y$ between weakly contractible objects is a weak equivalence
\item[(Cof-Mon)] For every cofibration $f : X \xhookrightarrow{} Y$ and for every object $Z$, the induced morphisms $id_Z \times f : Z \times X \xhookrightarrow{} Z \times Y$ $f \times id_Z : X \times Z \xhookrightarrow{} Y \times Z$ are cofibrations.
\item[(Sub)] For every pushout diagram of the form
    \[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\& W \& \\
	X \&\& Y \\
	\& Z
	\arrow[hook, from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow[hook, from=3-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
in $\mathcal{C}$, if $X,Y,Z$ are objects in $\mathcal{C}^{\times}$, then so is $W$.
\item[(Weq-Mon)] $\mathcal{C}^{\times}$ is a monoidal subcategory of $\mathcal{C}$ such that for every weak equivalence $f : X \xrightarrow[]{\sim} Y$ and every object $Z$ in $\mathcal{C}^{\times}$, the induced morphisms $id_Z \times f : Z \times X \xrightarrow{\sim} Z \times Y$ $f \times id_Z : X \times Z \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \times Z$ are weak equivalences as well.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
(Theorem 2.7 \cite{dandrea_quantum_2026})
The opposite category of $C^*$-algebras with unital $*$-homomorphisms as opposite morphisms, zero $C^*$-algebra as the initial object, $\mathbb{C}$ as the terminal object, surjective $*$-homomorphisms as cofibrations, $*$-homomorphisms inducing isomorphism on $K$-theory as weak equivalences, $\mathcal{N}_{max}$ as the distinguished subcategory and maximal tensor product is a cw-Waldhausen symmetric monoidal category denoted by $\mathcal{CpctQuant}^{\times}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The category of compact Hausdorff spaces with embeddings as cofibrations and $K$-equivalences as weak equivalences is a cw-Waldhausen category.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition 2.17]{dandrea_quantum_2026})
A finite quantum K-weak CW-complex is an object $X$ in the category $Ho(\mathcal{CpctQuant}^{\times})$ admitting a finite sequence of \textit{weak cofibrations} of the form

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\& {\tilde{X^{d_{k}}}} \& \\
	{X^{d_{k-1}}} \&\& {X^{d_{k}}}
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\sim"', from=2-3, to=1-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
such that $X^{d_0}$ is finite and the sequence is compatible with pushouts in $\mathcal{CpctQuant}^{\times}$ i.e.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& {\tilde{X^{d_k}}} & \\
	{X^{d_{k-1}}} && {\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{i_k} \mathbb{B}_i^{d_k}} \\
	& {\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{i_k} \mathbb{S}_i^{d_k}}
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\partial"', hook, from=3-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
(\cite[Section 4.2, Proposition 5.2]{hong_quantum_2002})
The graph corresponding to the odd-dimensional quantum real projective space $C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1})$ is given by $E= (\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_{n+1}\},\{e_{ij,jk} \ \vert \ 1\leq i \leq j \leq k \leq n+1 \}, r,s )$ where, $r(e_{ij,jk}) = v_k$ and $s(e_{ij,jk}) = v_i$, while the even-dimensional quantum real projective space $C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n})$ is given by $E= (\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_{n+1}\},\{e_{ij,jk} \ \vert \ 1\leq i \leq j \leq k \leq n+1 \text{ and } i \leq n \}, r,s )$ where, $r(e_{ij,jk}) = v_k$ and $s(e_{ij,jk}) = v_i$.
\label{rpga}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
The topological graph corresponding to the quantum odd real projective spaces $C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1})$ given by :
$E= (\{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{n}\} \sqcup S^1, \{e_{ij,jk} \  \vert \ 1 \leq i \leq j \leq k \leq n \} \sqcup_{1\leq i\leq n, i\leq j < n+1} X_{ij,jn+1},r,s) $ with $X_{ij,jn+1} \cong S^1$ and $r(e_{ij,jk}) = v_k, s(e_{ij,jk}) = v_i , r|_{X_{ij,jn+1}} = id_{S^1}, s(X_{ij,jn+1}) = v_i$.
\label{rp3ta}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Denote $B = C^*(F)$, where $F$ is the directed graph corresponding to $C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1})$ as given in Proposition \ref{rpga} and let $z_{X_{ij,jn+1}}$ be the unitary generator of $X_{ij,jn+1}$. Now consider the two maps:
$\psi^0 : C_0(E^0) \xrightarrow[]{} B$ and $\psi^1 : X_E \xrightarrow[]{} B$
\begin{align*}
   \psi^1((\delta_{e_{ij,jk}})) &\mapsto S_{e_{ij,jk}} \\
   \psi^1((z_{X_{ij,jn+1}})) &\mapsto S_{e_{ij,jn+1}} \\
   \psi^0((\delta_{v_{i}})) &\mapsto P_{v_i}  \\
   \psi^0(0,z) &\mapsto S_{e_{n+1n+1,n+1n+1}} \\
   \psi^0(0,1) &\mapsto P_{v_{n+1}} \\
\end{align*}
Observe that $\langle z_{X_{ij,jn+1}}, z_{X_{ij,jn+1}} \rangle_{C_0(E^0)} = (0,1_{S^1}) \in C_0(\{v_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \sqcup S^1)$, due to which it is routine to check that the conditions (1) and (2) for $(\psi^0, \psi^1)$ to be a representation hold. Furthermore, $E^0_{rg} = \{v_1,v_2,\dots, v_n\}$, so we need to check the covariance condition at $v_i$. Firstly, $\varphi_X(\delta_{v_i}) = id_{C_0(s^{-1}(v_i)}$ so,
\begin{align*}
    \psi^{(1)}(id_{C_0(s^{-1}(v_i))}) &= \psi^{(1)}(\sum \theta_{\delta_{e_{ij,jk}},\delta_{e_{ij,jk}}} + \sum \theta_{z_{X_{ij,jn+1}},z_{X_{ij,jn+1}}}) \\
                                 &= \sum S_{e_{ij,jk}}S_{e_{ij,jk}}^* + \sum S_{e_{ij,jn+1}} S_{e_{ij,jn+1}}^* \\
                                 &= P_{v_i} \\
                                 &= \psi^0(\delta_{v_i})
\end{align*}

So we have that $(\psi^0, \psi^1)$ is a covariant representation of the given topological graph. So by universality, we have a $*$-homomorphism $\mu : C^*(E) \xrightarrow[]{} C^*(F)$.

Furthermore, the topological graph $E$ is topologically free as it has no base points of loops without exits. So $\mu$ is injective when it is restricted to $C_0(E^0)$ and the graph is topologically free, so by Cuntz-Krieger uniqueness theorem for topological graphs, we have that $\mu$ is injective everywhere. Furthermore, as all generators of the codomain are in the image of $\mu$, it is also surjective and we are done.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
The topological graph for $C(S_q^{2n+1})$ is given by $(\{v_1,\dots,v_n \} \sqcup S^1, \{e_{ij} | 1\leq i \leq j \leq n \} \sqcup_{i=1}^{n} X_{in+1} , r, s)$, with $X_{in+1} \cong S^1$ and $r\vert_{X_{in+1}} = id_{S^1}$, $r(e_{ij}) = v_j$ and $s(e_{ij}) = s(X_{in+1}) = v_i$, while for $C(B_q^{2n+1})$, it is given by the quadruple $(\{v_1,\dots,v_n \} \sqcup [-1,1], \{e_{ij} | 1\leq i \leq j \leq n \} \sqcup_{i=1}^{n} Y_{in+1} , r, s)$, with $Y_{in+1} \cong [-1,1]$ and $r\vert_{Y_{in+1}} = id_{[-1,1]}$, $r(e_{ij}) = v_j$ and $s(e_{ij}) = s(Y_{in+1}) = v_i$
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
For brevity we adopt the following convention that $f_{ij,jk}$ denotes an element in $C(X_{ij,jk})$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
The commutative diagram \ref{realeven} is a pullback diagram.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This pullback diagram is a special case of the covariant functoriality of graph algebras proven by \cite{hajac_covariant_2024} (See Example 5.3).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
(\cite[Proposition 5.1]{hong_quantum_2002})
The graph of $C(S_q^{2n})$ consists of vertices $\{v_i\}_{i=1}^n \sqcup \{w_1,w_2\}$ and edges $\{e_{ij} \vert 1 \leq i \leq j  < n\} \sqcup \{g_{i,k} \vert 1 \leq i \leq n, k = 1,2\}$ with $s(e_{ij}) = s(g_{ik}) = v_i$ and $r(e_{ij}) = v_j, r(g_{ik}) = w_k$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
There is a exact sequence of $C^*$-algebras:
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	0 & {\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1)} & {C(B_q^{2n+1})} & {C(S_q^{2n})} & 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
More explicitly, $ker\alpha = \langle t^0(f) \vert f \in C_0(-1,1) \rangle$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The $*$-homomorphism $\alpha$ is induced by the factor map $m^0 : \{v_i\} \sqcup \{-1,1\} \xrightarrow[]{} \{v_i\} \sqcup [-1,1]$ and $m^1 : \{e_{ij,jk} \} \sqcup \{-1,1\}_{in+1} \xrightarrow[]{} \{e_{ij,jk}\} \sqcup Y_{in+1}$. Note that here, we rewrite $\{w_1,w_2\}$ as $\{-1,1\}$ and $g_{i,k}$ as $\{-1,1\}_{in+1}$ as to emphasise the embedding of the final vertices and edges inside the closed interval. So by \cite[Proposition 4.1]{gothe_gluing_2026} we have that the admissible pair corresponding to the (gauge-invariant) ideal $ker\alpha$ is $\{v_i\} \sqcup \{-1,1\}, \{-1,1\}$.

Consider the subset $V = (-1,1) \subseteq E^0$. This is a hereditary and saturated subset of $E^0$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{hss}), so we have that $S(H(V)) = V$. By Proposition 6.1 of \cite{katsura_class_2006-1}, we have that for the ideal generated by $t^0(C_0(V))$ is gauge-invariant, and the admissible pair is given by $(E^0 \backslash S(H(V)) , E^0_{sg}\backslash S(H(V))$, which in this case gives the admissible pair $(\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\} \sqcup \{-1,1\} , \{-1,1\}$. So by the bijective correspondence between gauge-invariant ideals and admissible pairs, we have that $ker\alpha = \langle t^0(f) | f\in C_0(-1,1) \rangle$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
(\cite[Proposition 5.2]{hong_quantum_2002})
The map $\beta: C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n}) \xhookrightarrow{} C(S_q^{2n})$ is given by:
\begin{align*}
    P_{v_i} &\mapsto P_{v_i} \hspace{2cm} i < n+1 \\
    P_{v_{n+1}} &\mapsto P_{w_1} + P_{w_2} \\
    S_{e_{ij,jk}} &\mapsto S_{e_{ij}}S_{e_{jk}} \hspace{2cm} k \neq n+1 \\
    S_{e_{ij,jn+1}} &\mapsto S_{e_{i,i+k-1}} (S_{g_{i+k-1,1}} + S_{g_{i+k-1,2}}) \\
    S_{f_{i,n+2-i}} &\mapsto S_{g_{i,1}} - S_{g_{i,-1}}
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
The following commutative diagram is a pullback diagram, yielding the quantum CW-complex structure for quantum real projective spaces $\mathbb{C} \twoheadleftarrow{} C(\mathbb{R}P_q^1) \twoheadleftarrow{} C(\mathbb{R}P_q^2) \twoheadleftarrow{} \dots \twoheadleftarrow{} C(\mathbb{R}P_q^n)$
    \[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\& {C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1})} \\
	{C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n})} \&\& {C(B_q^{2n+1})} \\
	\& {C(S_q^{2n})}
	\arrow["\gamma"', two heads, from=1-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\delta", hook', from=1-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\beta"', hook', from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["\alpha", two heads, from=2-3, to=3-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
The $*$-homomorphisms $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are given in the following lemmas.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
The map $\delta : C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1}) \xrightarrow[]{} C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1})$ given by:

\begin{align*}
   t^1((\delta_{e_{ij,jk}})) &\mapsto t^1((\delta_{e_{ij}}))t^1((\delta_{e_{jk}})) \\
   t^1(f_{ij,jn+1}) &\mapsto t^1(\delta_{e_{ij}})t^1(f_{jn+1})  \\
   t^1(f_{i n+1,n+1 n+1}) &\mapsto t^1(f_{in+1}) \\
   t^0((\delta_{v_{i}})) &\mapsto t^0(\delta_{v_i})  \\
   t^0(0,f) &\mapsto t^0(0,f)
\end{align*}
is injective. Here we use the fact that, $q : [-1,1] \xrightarrow[]{} S^1 $ is continuous surjective map by identifying the end points induces an injective embedding $C(S^1) \xhookrightarrow{} C[-1,1]$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1})$ is topologically free and $\delta |_{C_0(E^0)}$ is injective, so by Cuntz-Krieger uniqueness theorem, $\delta$ is injective everywhere.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
Let $E$ be the directed graph corresponding to $C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n})$ as given in Proposition \ref{rpga} and $F$ be the topological graph corresponding to $C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1})$ as in Lemma \ref{rp3ta}. Then the maps $m^0 : E^0 \xrightarrow[]{} F^0$ and $m^1 : E^1 \xrightarrow[]{} F^1$, be given by:
\begin{align*}
    m^0(v_i) &= v_i \hspace{3cm} i \neq n+1 \\
    m^0(v_{n+1}) &= \{1\} (\in S^1) \\
    m^1(e_{ij,jk}) &= e_{ij,jk} \\
    m^1(e_{ij,jn+1}) &= \{1\} (\in X_{ij,jn+1}) \\
\end{align*}
gives a injective regular factor map, and consequently we have a surjective $*$-homomorphism $\gamma: C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n+1}) \xrightarrow[]{} C(\mathbb{R}P_q^{2n})$, with $ker\gamma = \langle t^0(f) \vert f \in C_0(S^1\backslash\{1\})\rangle$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
It is easy to check that $(m^0,m^1)$ is a proper factor map, combined with the fact that $E^0_{rg} = F^0_{rg} = \{v_1, v_2, \dots ,v_n\}$, makes it a regular factor map. Now by \cite[Lemma 4.1 ]{gothe_gluing_2026}, the invariant subset corresponding to the ideal $ker\gamma$ is $\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n,1\}$.
    
$V = S^1 \backslash \{1\}$ is a saturated and hereditary subset of $E^0$. And by the same argument of Proposition \ref{hsker}, the result follows.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Proof of the theorem

    The Pedersen conditions are:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $ker\delta \cap ker\gamma = 0$
        
        $\delta$ is injective.
        
        \item $\beta^{-1}(\alpha(C(B_q^{2n+1}))) = \gamma(C(RP_q^{2n+1})$
        
        $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ are surjective.
        
        \item $\delta(ker \gamma) = ker\alpha$
        
        Let, $a \in ker\alpha$, then say $a = t^n(\xi)t^0(f)t^m(\eta)^*$. If $\xi = \xi_1\otimes \xi_2 \otimes \dots \otimes \xi_n$, then,  $a = t^1(\xi_1)t^1(\xi_2)\dots t^1(\xi_n) t^0(f) t^m(\eta)^*$. But $t^1(\xi_n)t^0(f) = t^1(\xi_n \cdot f)$ and as $f \in C_0(-1,1)$ and $r = id$, we have that $\xi_n \in C_0(-1,1)$ and by construction of $\delta$, it is routine computation to check that image of $\delta$ will contain all paths ending in $(-1,1)$. Similar result holds for $t^m(\eta)^*$, and as we have that the generator of $ker\gamma$ maps to generator of $ker \alpha$, we have that $ker \alpha \subseteq \delta(ker\gamma)$ and we are done. The other subset inequality follows from the commutativity of the diagram.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
(\cite{pedersen_pullback_1999})
Let $I$ be a finite indexing set and $\pi_j^i : A_i \xrightarrow[]{} A_{ij} \ \  i,j \in I$ and $A_{ij} = A_{ji}$ be a set of $*$-homomorphisms between $C^*$-algebras. Then the multipullback $C^*$-algebra $\oplus_{ij}A_i$ is the categorical wide pullback of the diagram defined by the $*$-homomorphisms. Alternatively, $\oplus_{ij}A_i$ can be defined as the $C^*$-algebra : $\oplus_{ij}A_i = \{ (a_1,\dots,a_i,\dots,a_j,\dots) \in \oplus A_i \ \vert \ \pi_j^i(a_i) = \pi_i^j(a_j) \}$
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition 3.2]{hajac_k-theory_2018})
 Let $I_i = \langle 1-t_it_i^*\rangle$ and let $I_{ij} = I_i + I_j$. Finally, let the quotient algebra be denoted by $B_i = \mathcal{T}^{n+1} / I_i$ and $B_{ij} = \mathcal{T}^{n+1} / I_{ij} $
 \begin{align*}
     \sigma_i &:  \mathcal{T}^{n+1} \twoheadrightarrow B_i \\
     \pi_j^i &: B_i \twoheadrightarrow B_{ij} 
 \end{align*}
 then the \textit{(untwisted) multipullback odd sphere} is defined as the multipullback $C^*$-algebra:
 \[
 C(S_H^{2n+1}) := \{ (b_0, b_1, \dots, b_n) \in \bigoplus B_i \vert \pi_j^i(b_i) = \pi_i^j(b_j) \text{ for all } 0 \leq i<j \leq n \} 
 \]
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
(\cite[Theorem 3.3]{hajac_k-theory_2018})
The multipullback odd sphere $C^*$-algebra $C^*(S_H^{2n+1})$ is generated by a set of generators - $\{s_0,s_1,\dots,s_n\}$ such that the following conditions hold:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $s_i^*s_i = 1$
    \item $s_is_j = s_js_i$ 
    \item $s_is_j^* = s_j^*s_i$ \hspace{3cm} $i \neq j$
    \item $\prod (1-s_is_i^*) = 0$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
(\cite[Lemma 5.1]{hajac_k-theory_2018})
The following is a short exact sequence:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	0 \& {\mathcal{K}} \& {\mathcal{T}^n} \& {C(S_H^{2n-1})} \& 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\sigma_n}", two heads, from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where $\sigma_n(t_i) = s_i$.
\label{bdos}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
Let $C(S_H^{2n})$ be the quotient $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1] / I$, called the even-dimensional multipullback quantum spheres.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
$C^*(s_0,s_1,\dots,s_n)$ be the $C^*$-algebra generated by a set of elements $s_0, s_1 , s_2, \dots , s_n$ satisfying the relations:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $s_i s_j = s_j s_i$
    \item $s_i^* s_j = s_j s_i^*$ for $ i < j$
    \item $s_i^*s_i = 1$ for $ i < n$
    \item $\prod (1-s_is_i^*) = 0$
    \item $s_n = s_n^*$ and $||s_n|| \leq 1$
\end{enumerate}
then we have that $C(S_H^{2n}) \cong C^*(s_0,s_1,\dots,s_n)$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $\sigma : \mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1] \xrightarrow[]{} C^*(s_0,s_1,\dots,s_n)$ be the following map:
\begin{align*}
    \sigma(t_i) &= s_{i} \\
    \sigma(z) &= s_n
\end{align*}

This is clearly a $^*$-homomorphism, and the kernel is the ideal generated by the element $\prod (1-t_it_i^*)(1-z^2)$, which is isomorphic to $\mathcal{K} \otimes C_0(-1,1)$ so we have the required isomorphism between $C(S_H^{2n})$ and $C^*(s_0,s_1,\dots,s_n)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
(\cite[Definition 6.1]{hong_quantum_2002},\cite[Proposition 2.1]{hong_noncommutative_2008},  \cite[Definition 4.1]{chakraborty_quantum_2011})
 Let $A$ be a unital $C^*$-algebra. Then the quantum double suspension $\Sigma^2A$ of $A$, is the $C^*$-subalgebra of $A \otimes \mathcal{T}$ generated by the elements $a \otimes p$ and $1 \otimes s$, where $s$ is the isometry generating $\mathcal{T}$ and $p = 1-ss^*$
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
By definition we have that $\Sigma^2C(B_q^n) = C(B_q^{2n+2})$ and $\Sigma^2C(S_q^n) = C(S_q^{2n+2})$ \cite{hong_noncommutative_2008}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
Let the following be 1-surjective pullback of unital $C^*$-algebras. 
\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\& X \& \\
	A \&\& B \\
	\& C
	\arrow["\delta", two heads, from=1-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\gamma"', from=1-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\alpha", from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["\beta"', two heads, from=2-3, to=3-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
Then the induced diagram on the quantum double suspensions is also a pullback diagram, viz, $\Sigma^2 X \cong \Sigma^2A \bigoplus_{\Sigma^2C} \Sigma^2B$.
\label{qdsp}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
If $\mu : A \xrightarrow[]{} B$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism between unital $C^*$-algebras, then the induced map between the quantum double suspensions is given by $\Sigma^2\mu : \Sigma^2A \xrightarrow[]{} \Sigma^2B$: $\Sigma^2\mu(a \otimes p) = \mu(a) \otimes p$ and $\Sigma^2 (1 \otimes s) = 1 \otimes s$. As $\mathcal{T}$ is a nuclear and hence an exact $C^*$-algebra, it is not difficult to check that pullbacks are preserved under the quantum double suspension endofunctor.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
We have the following pullback diagram

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	{C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1})} \& {\mathcal{T}^n\otimes C[-1,1]} \\
	{C(\mathbb{S}_q^{2n})} \& {C(S_H^{2n})}
	\arrow[hook, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For n = 0, this is clearly a pullback diagram as $C(B_q^1) = C[-1,1]$.


For higher dimension we proceed using induction. Consider the following diagram:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	{C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1})} \& {\Sigma^2(\mathcal{T}^{n-1}\otimes C[-1,1])} \& {\mathcal{T}^n\otimes C[-1,1]} \\
	{C(\mathbb{S}_q^{2n})} \& {\Sigma^2(C(S_H^{2n-2}))} \& {C(S_H^{2n})}
	\arrow[hook, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]


The induction hypothesis is that the following diagram is a pullback:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	{C(B_q^{2n-1})} \& {\mathcal{T}^{n-1}\otimes C[-1,1]} \\
	{C(S_q^{2n-2})} \& {C(S_H^{2n-2})}
	\arrow[hook, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

So by Proposition \ref{qdsp}, the following is also a pullback:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	{\Sigma^2C(B_q^{2n-1})} \& {\Sigma^2(\mathcal{T}^{n-1}\otimes C[-1,1])} \\
	{\Sigma^2C(S_q^{2n-2})} \& {\Sigma^2(C(S_H^{2n-2}))}
	\arrow[hook, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[two heads, from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
which gives us that the left square is a pullback.

We know that the following is a short exact sequence:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	0 \& {\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1)} \& {\mathcal{T}^{n-1}\otimes C[-1,1]} \& {C(S_H^{2n-2})} \& 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\alpha", two heads, from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]

So the induced map on the quantum double suspensions is $\Sigma^2\alpha : \Sigma^2(\mathcal{T}^{n-1} \otimes C[-1,1] \xrightarrow[]{} \Sigma^2C(S_H^{2n-2})$ is $\Sigma^2\alpha(t_0 \otimes 1) = t_0 \otimes 1$ and $\Sigma^2\alpha((1-t_0t_0^*) \otimes a) = (1-t_0t_0^*) \otimes \alpha(a)$. Clearly, we have that $\iota(ker\alpha) = ker\Sigma^2\alpha$, so the right square is pullback, consequently, by pasting lemma, the outer square is also a pullback.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
The inclusion $\iota : C(B_q^{2n+1}) \xhookrightarrow{} \mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1]$ induces an isomorphism on K-theory.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The $K$-theory of $\mathcal{T}$ is free and abelian, so by Kunneth formula for $C^*$-algebras \cite[Theorem 2.14]{schochet_topological_1982}, we have the isomorphism $K_{*}(\mathcal{T} \otimes C[-1,1]) \cong K_{*}(\mathcal{T}) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} K_*(C[-1,1])$ and consequently we have $K_0(\mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1]) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $K_1(\mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1]) \cong \{0\}$ and is generated by class of identity i.e. $[1]_0$. Furthermore, the $K$-theory of $C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1})$ is given by $K_0(C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ generated by the class of identity \cite[Proposition 4.1]{hong_noncommutative_2008} and $K_1(C(B_q^{2n+1})) = \{0\}$. The inclusion $C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1}) \xhookrightarrow{} \mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1]$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism, so it induces an isomorphism on $K$-theory.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
The inclusion $ \mu: C(S_q^{2n}) \xhookrightarrow{} C(S_H^{2n})$ also induces an isomorphism on $K$-theory.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
To begin with have the inclusion map $C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1}) \xhookrightarrow{} \mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1]$ and two short exact sequences:

\[\begin{tikzcd}
	0 & {\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1)} & {C(\mathbb{B}_q^{2n+1})} & {C(S_q^{2n})} & 0 \\
	0 & {\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1)} & {\mathcal{T}^n\otimes C[-1,1]} & {C(S_H^{2n})} & 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["id", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[hook, from=1-4, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]

So we have the following induced maps between the six term sequences in $K$-theory

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&,cramped,sep=tiny]
	\&\& {K_0(\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1))} \&\& \\
	\&\& {K_0(\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1))} \\
	{K_0(\mathcal{T}^n\otimes C[-1,1])} \& {K_0(C(B_q^{2n+1}))} \&\& {K_1(C(S_q^{2n}))} \& {K_1(C(S^{2n}_H)} \\
	{K_0(C(S_H^{2n}))} \& {K_0(C(S_q^{2n}))} \&\& {K_1(C(B_q^{2n+1}))} \& {K_1(\mathcal{T}^n \otimes C[-1,1])} \\
	\&\& {K_1(\mathcal{K}\otimes C_0(-1,1))} \\
	\\
	\&\& {K_1(\mathcal{K} \otimes C_0(-1,1))}
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=4-1]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=4-2]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=3-5, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=7-3]
	\arrow[from=4-2, to=4-1]
	\arrow[from=4-2, to=5-3]
	\arrow[from=4-4, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=4-4, to=4-5]
	\arrow[from=4-5, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=5-3, to=4-4]
	\arrow[from=5-3, to=7-3]
	\arrow[from=7-3, to=4-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
which becomes

\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& 0 &&&& 0 & \\
	{\mathbb{Z}} && 0 && {\mathbb{Z}} && {K_1(C(S_H^{2n}))} \\
	{\mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}} && 0 && {K_0(C(S_H^{2n}))} && 0 \\
	& {\mathbb{Z}} &&&& {\mathbb{Z}}
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-6]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-6, to=2-5]
	\arrow[curve={height=12pt}, from=2-1, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[curve={height=-12pt}, from=2-3, to=2-7]
	\arrow[from=2-5, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=2-7, to=1-6]
	\arrow[curve={height=-12pt}, from=3-1, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=4-2]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[curve={height=12pt}, from=3-3, to=3-7]
	\arrow[from=3-5, to=4-6]
	\arrow[from=3-7, to=2-7]
	\arrow[from=4-2, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=4-2, to=4-6]
	\arrow[from=4-6, to=3-7]
\end{tikzcd}\]

Clearly, we have that $K_1(C(S_H^{2n})) = 0$, so $\mu_1$ is an isomorphism. Moreover, we have the following:

\[\begin{tikzcd}
	0 & {\mathbb{Z}} & {\mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}} & {\mathbb{Z}} & 0 \\
	0 & {\mathbb{Z}} & {K_0(C(S_H^{2n}))} & {\mathbb{Z}} & 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\cong", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow["\cong", from=1-4, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]

The left and right arrows are isomorphisms, so by Short Five Lemma we have that $\mu_0$ is also an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Note that the last line of the proof also says that $\mathcal{T}^n\otimes C[-1,1]$ is $K$-ball and $C(S^{2n}_H)$ is its boundary $K$-sphere.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
Let $A_i$ and $A_{ij}$ where $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ be finite families of $C^*$-algebras with the following $*$-homomorphisms from a $C^*$-algebra $X$: 

$\pi_i : X \xrightarrow[]{} A_i$

$\pi_{j}^i : A_i \xrightarrow[]{} A_{ij}$ 

which form a star-shaped commutative diagram centred at 2 as below:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\&\& X \&\& \\
	{A_1} \&\& {A_2} \&\& {A_3} \\
	\& {A_{12}} \&\& {A_{23}}
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=2-5, to=3-4]
\end{tikzcd}\]

then this is a multipullback diagram of $C^*$-algebras i.e. the induced map $\sigma : X \xrightarrow[]{} \bigoplus_{ij} A_i$ given by $\sigma(x) = (\pi_i(x))_i$ is an isomorphism iff

the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\bigcap_{j \in I} ker\pi_j = \{0\}$
    \item $\pi_2(X) = \bigcap_{j \neq 2} (\pi_j^2)^{-1}(\pi_2^j(A_j))$
    \item $ker \pi_2^k = \pi_k(\bigcap_{p \neq k} ker \pi_p)$ for all $k \neq 2$
\end{enumerate}
\label{multi}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This proof is heavily based on the original proof by Pedersen in \cite[Proposition 3.1]{pedersen_pullback_1999} for a pullback of $C^*$-algebras, and as has been adapted here to the case of a multipullback of $C^*$-algebras.


First let us assume the three conditions hold.

Then $\sigma : X \xrightarrow[]{} \bigoplus_{ij} A_i$ maps $x \mapsto (\pi_i(x))_i$. 

Say we have a $x \in X$ such that $\sigma(x) = 0$, then $\pi_i(x) = 0$ for all $i$, then $x$ is in $\bigcap_{j \in I} ker\pi_j$ which is the singleton $\{0\}$, so we have that $\sigma$ is injective.

For surjectivity,

say $(a_i)_{i\in I}$, theb

\begin{align*}
    a_2 &\in (\pi_j^2)^{-1} (\pi_i^j(a_j)) \\
    a_2 &\in (\pi_j^2)^{-1} (\pi_i^j(A_j))
\end{align*}
So by (2) we have that $a_2 = \pi_2(x)$ for some $x \in X$. Now consider $k \neq i$.

\begin{align*}
    \pi_2^k(a_k - \pi_k(x)) &= \pi_2^k(a_k) - \pi_2^k(\pi_k(x)) \\
                            &= \pi_k^i(a_2) - \pi_k^2(\pi_i(x)) \\
                            &= 0
\end{align*}

We have that
\begin{align*}
    a_k - \pi_k(x) &\in ker\pi_2^k \\
    a_k - \pi_k(x) &= \pi_k(y_k) \hspace{2cm} \text{ for some } y_k \in \bigcap_{p \neq k} ker \pi_p
\end{align*}

Clearly, we have that $\sigma( x + \Sigma_k y_k) = (a_i)$ and we conclude that $\sigma$ is surjective.

For the implication in the other direction:

Let $x \in \bigcap_{j \in I} ker \pi_j$, then $\sigma(x) = 0$, but as $\sigma$ is injective, we have that $x = 0$ and we get that (1) is satisfied.

Let $\sigma$ be surjective, then to see that (2) holds, we observe that,

if $a_2 = \pi_2(x)$ for some $x \in X$, then $\pi_j^i(a_2) = \pi_2^j(\pi_j(x)) \implies a_2 \in (\pi_j^2)^{-1}(\pi_2^j(A_j))$ and if $a_i \in (\pi_j^2)^{-1}(\pi_2^j(A_j))$, then $(a_i)_i \in \oplus_{ij} A_i$, so by surjectivity of $\sigma$ we have that $a_2 = \pi_2(x)$ for some $x \in X$.

Now if
\begin{align*}
     &a_k \in ker \pi_2^k \\
    \implies &\pi_2^k(a_k) = 0 \\
    \implies &(0,\dots,a_k,0,\dots 0) \in \oplus_{ij}A_i \\
    \implies &\exists x \in X \ni \pi_k(x) = a_k \text{ and } \pi_p(x) = 0 \ \forall \ p \neq x
\end{align*}

The other inequality for (3) follows easily.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
The $C^*$-algebra $C(S_H^{2n})$ is isomorphic to the wide pullback $\sigma_{-1} : \mathcal{T}^n \xrightarrow[]{} C(S^{2n-1}_H)$, $\sigma_{1} : \mathcal{T}^n \xrightarrow[]{} C(S^{2n-1}_H)$ and $ev_{-1} : C(S_H^{2n-1})\otimes C[-1,1] \xrightarrow[]{} C(S^{2n-1}_H)$ and $ev_{1} : C(S_H^{2n-1})\otimes C[-1,1] \xrightarrow[]{} C(S^{2n-1}_H)$ in the following manner:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
	\&\& {C(S_H^{2n})} \&\& \\
	{\mathcal{T}^n} \&\& {C(S_H^{2n-1}) \otimes C[-1,1]} \&\& {\mathcal{T}^n} \\
	\& {C(S^{2n-1}_H)} \&\& {C(S^{2n-1}_H)}
	\arrow["{\pi_1}"', two heads, from=1-3, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_2}", two heads, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\pi_3}", two heads, from=1-3, to=2-5]
	\arrow["{\sigma_{-1}}", two heads, from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["{ev_{-1}}"', two heads, from=2-3, to=3-2]
	\arrow["{ev_1}", two heads, from=2-3, to=3-4]
	\arrow["{\sigma_1}"', two heads, from=2-5, to=3-4]
\end{tikzcd}\]
where the maps $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_{-1}$ are the $\sigma_n$ as in Proposition \ref{bdos} and the maps $\pi_i$ are defined as:

\begin{align*}
    \pi_1(s_i) &= t_i \hspace{3cm} 0 \leq i < n\\
    \pi_1(s_n) &= -1\\
    \pi_2(s_i) &= s_i \otimes 1 \hspace{3cm} 0 \leq i < n\\
    \pi_2(s_n) &= 1 \otimes z\\
    \pi_3(s_i) &= t_i \hspace{3cm} 0 \leq i < n\\
    \pi_3(s_n) &= 1\\
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We need to check that conditions (1)-(3) of Proposition \ref{multi} are satisfied.

(1) 

$ker\pi_1$ is the ideal generated by $(1+s_n)$, $ker\pi_3$ is the ideal generated by $(1-s_n)$ while the kernel of $\pi_2$ is generated by $\prod_{0 \leq i <n}(1-s_is_i^*)$. So as $s_n$ is central, we have that $\bigcap ker\pi_i = \langle\prod (1-s_is_i^*)(1-s_n^2) \rangle$ which is $0$ by the last generating relation of $C(S^{2n}_H)$.

(2)

All the maps are surjective, so this condition follows trivially.

(3)
$ker\pi_2 \cap ker\pi_3$ is inside the ideal generated by $(1-s_n)\prod(1-s_is_i^*)$ which maps to $2\prod(1-s_is_i^*) = ker\sigma_{-1}$. Furthermore, if $a \in \langle \prod (1-t_it_i^*) \rangle$ and due to surjectivity of $\pi_1$, we have that there exists a $b \in \langle \prod (1-s_is_i^*) \rangle$ such that $\pi_1(b) = a$, then consider the element $\pi_1(b(1-s_n)/2) = a$. $\pi_2 (\prod(1 - s_is_i^*)) = 0$ by the generating relation for $C(S_H^{2n-1})$, and $\pi_3(1-s_n) = 0$, so we have the other inequality.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
This shows that $C(S_H^{2n})$ is a $K$-weak suspension of $C(S_H^{2n-1})$, as $\mathcal{T}^n$ has the same $K$-theory as that of a point, and replacing $\mathcal{T}^n$ with the $C^*$-algebra of a  point i.e. $\mathbb{C}$ yields the usual suspension of $C^*$-algebras. Moreover, this construction yields a partial quantum CW-complex decomposition $C(S_H^{2n-1}) \twoheadleftarrow{} C(S_H^{2n})$ through gluing two $2n$-dimensional $K$-balls mirroring the classical construction.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
